extracted.intended_audience: academic scholars, students, and practitioners in film/communication/cultural studies
extracted.subtask_description: Applying Stuart Hall's encoding/decoding theoretical framework to analyze film communication, audience reception, and adapted films, with attention to production/reception variables and decoding positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encoding (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encoding refers to that the information disseminator transforming the conveyed message, meaning, intention or viewpoint, through verbal or non-verbal form, into a symbolic code or information form that has specific rules and is easy to understand and translate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encoding is organized through the operation of codes within the semantic chain of a discourse. It emphasizes the construction and coding of information; media encoders need a sufficient understanding of the target information (including anticipated audience decoding) so as to form 'an encoded message in the form of meaningful discourse' (Hall, 1973: 3). Encoding involves what producers consciously want to say but also 'takes into consideration complex factors of production that go well beyond simply the author’s intent' (Benshoff, 2015: 16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoding (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoding meant the process that the recipient of the information interprets the code, and/or recreates the conveyed ideology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decoding/interpretation activities of decoders reflect communication complexity and social diversity; receivers play an active role, can reproduce meaning via feedback, and may understand, accept, resist, or reinterpret encoded meanings based on their frameworks and contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal and external factors influencing encoding
rubrics_metrics.description: The formation of information (encoding) is influenced by three main factors, categorized into internal factors (practitioner’s own knowledge structure, occupational morality, professional standards and concepts) and external factors (production relations, institutional structure, industry mechanisms and rules, broadcasting methods and technical equipment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers' encoding choices are shaped by their knowledge, ethics and professional standards as well as by institutional and technical constraints; analyses should account for both sets of factors when evaluating encoded meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal and external factors influencing decoding
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoding is affected by internal factors (personal frameworks of knowledge, semantic habits, political tendencies, social and cultural positions, understandings of a text’s economic and technical infrastructure) and external factors (relations of production, technical infrastructure, social and cultural context, historical background, and differences in relationship/status between transmitter and audience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience interpretations will vary with cultural background, knowledge structure, social status, ideological understanding, economic status, values, decoding context, ethical and religious standpoints; these should be explicitly considered in reception studies, especially in transcultural contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model variables: frameworks of knowledge, relations of production, technical infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Hall's model highlights variables that exist on both encoder and decoder sides, involving their own 'frameworks of knowledge', 'relations of production', and 'technical infrastructure' (Benshoff, 2015: 15-16).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the model, identify and compare these variables on producer and audience sides to explain divergences or alignments between encoding and decoding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four stages of media discourse circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hall suggests stages analogous to commodity circulation: (1) production/encoding of meaning, (2) 'finished product' phase where meaning is embedded in text and enters circulation, (3) decoding stage where audiences interpret and generate effects, and (4) reproduction stage where audiences produce new interpretations/feedback or create new texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should track a film/text through these stages. The reproduction stage (audience-created texts/feedback) is highlighted as important but often underdeveloped and a site for further research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film as meaningful discourse (denotation and connotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Film text is a 'meaningful discourse' where the meaning conveyed has double levels—connotation and denotation—so various meaningful codes present to the public generate multilayered representations open to diverse responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate films not only for surface (denotative) content but for connotative, ideological layers; consider how audiovisual codes construct implicit and explicit messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant (preferred) decoding position
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominant decoding position: the decoder decodes the text according to how the encoder encoded it ('decoded in a manner highly aligned or symmetrical to that in which it had been encoded').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify when audiences accept the intended/hegemonic reading; analyze how production frames and dominant ideology facilitate this alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiated decoding position
rubrics_metrics.description: Negotiated position contains a mixture of adaptive and oppositional factors: the decoder understands the media's promoted meaning partly and interprets partly according to their own social background; they neither completely agree nor completely deny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for audience readings that accept aspects of the dominant message while adapting others to local or personal conditions (e.g., transcultural adaptations requiring 'global' understanding adjusted to 'local' contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppositional decoding position
rubrics_metrics.description: Oppositional decoding: audiences adopt a decoding position inconsistent with the dominant coding, decoding 'in a contrary way' and resisting the producer's intended meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate oppositional decoding (understanding then rejecting the intended meaning) from mere misunderstanding; evaluate social/ideological bases for oppositional readings and the role of media as a forum for challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aberrant decoding (failure of fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aberrant decoding reflects the lack of 'fit' between producers and audiences: audiences fail to understand the message because their socio-cultural positioning or ideologies differ from the producers (a deviation from sender intent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish cases where audience readings reflect ideological resistance (oppositional) from cases of incomprehension; consider cultural distance, knowledge gaps, and semantic habits as causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referential versus critical decoding
rubrics_metrics.description: Referential decoding regards the programme as 'applicable to real life' (connecting characters/program to real-world experience); critical decoding treats the programme as 'constructions consisting of messages and narrative formulae' and focuses on aesthetic/structural analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the referential/critical distinction as an operational standard for observing audience decoding: referential statements are affective and situate content in real life; critical statements are cognitive and address syntax, themes, and pragmatic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity and fluidity of decoding positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Hall proposed three major positions, actual audience decoding is more complicated: modes are connected, individuals may occupy multiple or shifting positions, and positions are not strictly determined by class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rigid classification; analyses should account for plurality, intra-individual variation, and context-dependent shifts in decoding strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical guidance for filmmakers/producers (improve reception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filmmakers/producers should concentrate on film content production aspects—film skills, story plot, theme meaning—and take into account the cultural psychology and aesthetic differences of audiences, attending to both local and international voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To improve audience decoding and reception, creators should integrate global/local perspectives, consider audience cultural backgrounds and aesthetic expectations, and design encoding (visual/technical codes) that anticipate varied decoding positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to adapted films (encoding/decoding across media)
rubrics_metrics.description: In adapted films, directors first 'read' and decode the original novels, then re-encode content into film language ('novel filmic encoding'); audiences (some familiar with the novel) may decode films based on their comprehension of the source text, leading to varied receptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating adaptations, analyze the double decoding/re-encoding process: how directors' interpretations transform source text codes into filmic codes and how audiences' prior knowledge shapes decoding and comparative judgments.
